name: Krasnikov Time Machine
description: Serguei Krasnikov's time machine of 1998, the Deutsch-Politzer spacetime with its metric multiplied by a conformal factor that sends its singular points to infinity, times a 2-sphere, inside a closed universe that is a Friedmann universe outside a layer round the equator of its 3-sphere. The region holding its closed timelike curves has no singularity, and the weak energy condition holds throughout.
convention: No factor of $c$ appears, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Serguei Krasnikov defined a region $L_N$ of a spacetime $N$ as a time machine when every event through which a closed causal curve passes lies inside it [krasnikov1998wec]. The rest of $N$, outside the causal future of $L_N$, had to be isometric to a causal spacetime $M$ outside the causal future of a compact region $L_M$, so that people who decide to build the machine live in $N$ and people who decide against it live in $M$ [krasnikov1998wec]. Krasnikov asked for $L_M$ to be compact to distinguish a machine that an advanced civilization might build from causality violations of a cosmological kind, such as the Gödel universe [krasnikov1998wec]. Stephen Hawking had shown that where causality violation with a compactly generated horizon grows from a noncompact initial surface, the averaged weak energy condition fails on that horizon [hawking1992, krasnikov1998wec]. Krasnikov looked for a machine whose horizon is not compactly generated, with neither a singularity nor any violation of the weak energy condition [krasnikov1998wec].¶Krasnikov started from the Deutsch-Politzer spacetime, which H. David Politzer described in 1992 as a flat plane with two segments, one later than the other, identified so that the region just before each joins the region just after the other [politzer1992, krasnikov1998wec]. Closed timelike curves run round the handle this makes, and the plane is flat except at the ends of the handle, two singular points with an excess angle of $2\pi$ [politzer1992]. Being flat, it needs no matter, and Krasnikov took it as proof that the weak energy condition can hold in a machine whose horizon is not compactly generated [krasnikov1998wec]. Andrew Chamblin, Gary Gibbons, and Alan Steif proved in 1994 that its metric cannot be smoothed out to an everywhere regular, asymptotically flat Lorentzian metric when the number of dimensions is even [chamblin1994].¶Krasnikov moved the singular points to infinity with a conformal factor, working first in two dimensions, since in four a factor that both kept the weak energy condition and freed the spacetime of singularities was hard to find [krasnikov1998wec]. On the square $|\tau|, |\chi| < m$ the metric is $ds^2 = f^{-2}(-d\tau^2 + d\chi^2)$, with $f$ a smooth bounded function that vanishes only at the four points $\tau = \pm h$, $\chi = \pm h$, where $0 < h < m/2$ [krasnikov1998wec]. The square is cut along the segments $\tau = \pm h$, $|\chi| < h$, which end at those points, the upper bank of each cut is glued to the lower bank of the other, and near the upper cut $f$ repeats its values near the lower one, $f(\tau, \chi) = f(\tau - 2h, \chi)$ [krasnikov1998wec]. Krasnikov called the result, with the four points removed, the curved Deutsch-Politzer time machine [krasnikov1998wec]. Its product with a 2-sphere of radius $R$ is the time machine $L_N$, and the weak energy condition holds in it when $R^{-2} \ge f(f_{,\chi\chi} - f_{,\tau\tau}) + f_{,\tau}^2 - f_{,\chi}^2$ at every point of the square [krasnikov1998wec].¶Krasnikov then placed $L_N$ in a closed universe on $\mathbb{R} \times S^3$, $ds^2 = a^2[-d\tau^2 + d\chi^2 + \rho^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\, d\phi^2)]$ with $-\pi/2 \le \chi \le \pi/2$, taking $a = 1/f$ and $\rho = fR$ on the square [krasnikov1998wec]. Off the square $a$ depends on $\tau$ alone and $\rho$ on $\chi$ alone, and where $|\chi|$ exceeds some $n$ between $m$ and $\pi/2$, $\rho = \cos\chi$ and the universe is a closed Friedmann universe [krasnikov1998wec]. Krasnikov considered that resemblance "only as a pleasant surprise" [krasnikov1998wec]. The weak energy condition holds outside $L_N$ as well, and the universe has cosmological singularities where $a = 0$, all of them outside $L_N$ [krasnikov1998wec]. In $L_N$ every inextendible timelike curve of bounded acceleration has infinite proper length, and every inextendible curve has infinite affine length in a parallel propagated frame, so that $L_N$ is free of singularities in two senses [krasnikov1998wec].¶Kengo Maeda, Akihiro Ishibashi, and Makoto Narita wrote in 1998 that the weak energy condition "does not necessarily prevent causality violations of the Deutsch-Politzer time machine type from occurring in classical general relativity", citing Krasnikov's model [maeda1998]. Assuming the strong energy and generic conditions, they proved that a chronology violating set of that type contains an incomplete causal geodesic, so that where such a set is causally geodesically complete, one of the two conditions fails [maeda1998]. They also proved that no such set forms in a maximal spacetime whose incomplete causal geodesics all end at singularities of the kind they called "non-naked", and saw in it support for chronology protection [maeda1998]. Krasnikov proved in 2002 that any spacetime $U$ has a maximal extension in which every closed causal curve, if there is one, lies in the chronological past of $U$ [krasnikov2002]. Krasnikov took the theorem to rule out, in classical general relativity, time machines "created by human beings", since a region prepared for one may equally evolve into a spacetime with no closed causal curve to its future [krasnikov2002]. Krasnikov's example is Misner space, whose acausal extension becomes causal once a single ray is removed and the metric is divided by a function that vanishes on it [krasnikov2002].¶John Earman, Christopher Smeenk, and Christian Wüthrich tested Krasnikov's definition in 2009 against their potency condition, under which every suitable extension of the region that a machine's instructions determine contains closed timelike curves [earman2009]. They showed that the definition is met with $L_N$ the causal future of a compact region, and that nothing then separates the operation of the machine from the closed timelike curves it is meant to make [earman2009]. They also tried a compact $L_N$ with the closed timelike curves in its causal future, and found the Deutsch-Politzer spacetime isometric to Minkowski space until after the machine has operated, so that Minkowski space continues it with no closed timelike curve [earman2009]. They judged it not obvious that Krasnikov's maximal extension of 2002 meets the form of the potency condition they preferred, with every extension required to be hole free [earman2009].

related.text: The closed Friedmann universe, whose metric Krasnikov's universe has wherever $|\chi| > n$, with $a$ a function of $\tau$ alone and $\rho = \cos\chi$ [krasnikov1998wec].

Another time machine whose matter obeys the weak energy condition. Amos Ori's model of 2005 has an empty torus at its core, wrapped in matter that obeys the dominant and strong energy conditions as well [ori2005].

The tube Krasnikov made in 1998 by changing the metric along a traveller's outward path. With it a round trip of any length might take an arbitrarily short time for an observer on Earth [krasnikov1998].

Minkowski space identified under a boost, with closed timelike curves beyond a horizon. Krasnikov pointed to it as a time machine whose compactness does not keep out singularities, a possible source of unpredictable information [krasnikov1998wec].

A traversable wormhole made into a time machine, which an advanced civilization able to create and maintain the wormhole might build. Whether the wormhole can be created and maintained turns in part on whether quantum fields obey an averaged weak energy condition [morris1988prl].

Two cosmic strings passing at high speed. Krasnikov classed the causality violation they make as cosmological, with that of the Gödel universe, and set both apart from a time machine an advanced civilization might build [krasnikov1998wec].
